prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Apply famous investors' frameworks to the publicly listed company "JPMORGAN CHASE & CO" (ticker JPM). Use the most recent information you know. Be specific (names, numbers, years). Never invent figures.
Reply with ONLY one JSON object:
{"summaries": { "<framework id>": "2-3 plain sentences on how well the company fits this investor's approach, written neutrally" } for EVERY framework below:
   "gardner": David Gardner: Rule Breaker Investing (The six Rule Breaker traits (Motley Fool Rule Breakers; “Rule Breakers, Rule Makers”, 1998))
   "buffett": Warren Buffett (Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters; tenets summarised in “The Warren Buffett Way” (Hagstrom))
   "munger": Charlie Munger (Munger's talks and “Poor Charlie's Almanack”)
   "lynch": Peter Lynch (“One Up on Wall Street” and “Beating the Street”)
   "fisher": Philip Fisher (“Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits” (the 15 points, condensed))
   "graham": Benjamin Graham (“The Intelligent Investor”, criteria for the defensive investor)
   "thiel": Peter Thiel (“Zero to One”: the seven questions every business must answer)
   "gerstner": Brad Gerstner (His public letters (e.g. “Time to Get Fit”, 2022) and interviews (BG2 podcast); a summary, not an official checklist)
   "druckenmiller": Stanley Druckenmiller (His public interviews and speeches; a summary, not an official checklist)
   "smith": Terry Smith (Fundsmith owner's manual and annual letters (“buy good companies, don't overpay, do nothing”))
   "greenblatt": Joel Greenblatt (“The Little Book That Beats the Market” (the Magic Formula))
   "akre": Chuck Akre (Akre's “three-legged stool”)
   "pabrai": Mohnish Pabrai (“The Dhandho Investor”)
   "wood": Cathie Wood (ARK Invest's published research (“Big Ideas”) on disruptive innovation)
   "ackman": Bill Ackman (Pershing Square's stated investment criteria (annual letters and presentations))
   "sleep": Nick Sleep (Nomad Investment Partnership letters (2001–2014))
   "valentine": Don Valentine (His talks (e.g. Stanford GSB, 2010) on what Sequoia looks for)
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?
   "g4": Is it run by great leaders and backed by smart, well-known investors or partners?
   "g6": Do commentators and analysts commonly call the stock overvalued (a trait Gardner sees as a good sign)?
   "simple": Is it an established business simple enough for a careful generalist to understand well?
   "b2": Has it shown consistent results over many years?
   "integrity": Is management honest and candid with shareholders, rational with capital, paid in a way that lines up with owners, and well governed?
   "b6": Does management avoid copying peers or empire-building for its own sake?
   "roic": Does it earn a high, consistent return on the capital it uses, without relying on debt?
   "fcf": Does it turn most of its profit into plenty of free cash flow?
   "b10": Has the money it kept (instead of paying out) grown the company's value by at least as much?
   "safety": Is the share price well below a conservative estimate of the business's value (a margin of safety)?
   "fairprice": Is the price reasonable for the quality and growth on offer?
   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?
   "ly2": Does it fit a clear category (fast grower, stalwart, turnaround…) with a simple story for its future?
   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?
   "runway": Can its sales keep growing substantially for many years, into new places or products?
   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?
   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?
   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?
   "gm": Is the gross margin high, a sign of pricing power?
   "fcfyield": Is the free-cash-flow yield reasonable or attractive for its quality and growth?
   "gb2": Is operating profit high compared with the whole company's value (enterprise value)?
   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM"}

summaries.gardner: JPMorgan is a 'Rule Maker' rather than a Rule Breaker: it is the top dog in US banking, but banking is not an emerging industry and its shares rose about 10% in the past year, half the market's gain. It has a strong brand and a celebrated leader in Jamie Dimon, but few of Gardner's disruptive-growth traits.
summaries.buffett: JPMorgan fits many Buffett tenets: a durable franchise with a low-cost deposit base, a candid and rational CEO whose shareholder letters Buffett has praised, a 20% return on tangible common equity in 2025 and EPS that more than tripled from $6.00 (2015) to $20.02 (2025). The drawbacks are the inherent leverage of banking and a price of about 3.1 times tangible book, a premium to peers that leaves little margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger was wary of banks because of leverage and opacity, but he respected Dimon's fortress-balance-sheet discipline, which carried JPMorgan through 2008 and 2023 stronger. Inverting, the main ways to fail are a severe credit cycle, a trading or cyber disaster, or a poor CEO succession.
summaries.lynch: JPMorgan is a Lynch stalwart with a simple story, the best-run big US bank, and a P/E of about 14. Its PEG of about 1.3 is fair rather than cheap, it is widely followed rather than overlooked, and its main shareholder-friendly feature is buybacks that cut diluted shares from 3,087.4M in 2020 to 2,781.5M in 2025.
summaries.fisher: JPMorgan scores well on Fisher's points about management depth, sales strength (No. 1 in US deposits, card spending and investment-banking fees) and continual investment in new products and technology (about $19.8B of tech spending planned for 2026). Banks have no R&D and margins depend on rates, which makes some of Fisher's 15 points hard to apply.
summaries.graham: JPMorgan passes Graham's size, earnings-stability and dividend-record tests and grew EPS far more than one third in ten years. It narrowly fails the valuation tests: a P/E of about 14-17 depending on the earnings base and a P/E times P/B of about 36, versus his limit of 22.5.
summaries.thiel: JPMorgan is a scale leader in an old industry rather than a Thiel-style creator of something new: it has no technology ten times better than rivals and no 'secret'. Its strengths on Thiel's list are distribution, a world-class team and a durable position.
summaries.gerstner: JPMorgan is not a natural Gerstner holding, though its large AI and technology budget and Kinexys blockchain payments show it adopting new technology. At about 13 times forward earnings it is reasonably priced, but its revenue growth is tied to rates and capital markets rather than a technology wave.
summaries.druckenmiller: JPMorgan is highly sensitive to the things Druckenmiller watches most, interest rates, the yield curve, credit and liquidity, and capital-markets activity has boosted results in 2026 (revenue of $157.4B in the first nine months). Whether it is a big position depends on his macro view; earnings growth is solid rather than accelerating sharply.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith avoids banks because their returns depend on leverage and their assets are hard to assess, so JPMorgan falls outside his approach despite its industry-leading 20% ROTCE. Gross margin and free cash flow, his key measures, do not apply cleanly to a bank.
summaries.greenblatt: Greenblatt's Magic Formula excludes financial companies, because return on capital and EV/EBIT are not meaningful for a bank. On simple measures JPMorgan's earnings yield of about 7% and 17-20% return on equity would look good.
summaries.akre: JPMorgan has two strong legs of Akre's stool: a business that earns about 20% on tangible equity and an exceptional, owner-minded management under Jamie Dimon. The reinvestment leg is weaker, because the bank returns most profits (an 82% net payout over the 12 months to end-2025) rather than compounding them internally.
summaries.pabrai: JPMorgan offers relatively low risk for a bank, but there is no temporary crisis or deep discount that would create a Dhandho opportunity today. Pabrai has been willing to buy banks after shocks, when fear makes them cheap, which is not the case at about 3.1 times tangible book.
summaries.wood: JPMorgan is an incumbent that ARK's research often sees as threatened by digital wallets, stablecoins and DeFi, even though it runs its own blockchain unit, Kinexys. It does not fit Cathie Wood's disruptive-innovation approach.
summaries.ackman: JPMorgan is a dominant, well-run franchise with high barriers to entry, but banks are leveraged, sensitive to interest rates and harder to predict than the simple, free-cash-flow-generative businesses Pershing Square prefers. At a premium to peers on tangible book, it also lacks the discount Ackman looks for.
summaries.sleep: JPMorgan does share some scale benefits with customers through its branch network, apps and pricing, and its deposit share rose from 8.1% in 2015 to 11.1% in 2025. It is not a classic 'scale economies shared' model like Costco or Amazon, but its scale advantage is growing.
summaries.valentine: JPMorgan solves the large, everyday problem of storing, moving and lending money safely, but it is a mature, highly regulated bank rather than a new, technology-driven market. It sits outside Don Valentine's venture-style approach.

momentum.evidence: JPMorgan shares rose 10.15% in the 52 weeks to Oct 13, 2026 (close $331.43), behind the SPY S&P 500 ETF's 20.42% one-year total return.

g4.evidence: Jamie Dimon, CEO since 2005, is widely regarded as the best bank CEO of his generation, and Berkshire Hathaway was a shareholder for years.

g6.evidence: Some commentators call JPMorgan expensive at about 3.1 times tangible book, a record premium to peers, but its P/E of about 14 is modest.

simple.evidence: Taking deposits and lending is easy to understand, but a $5 trillion universal bank with trading, derivatives and complex capital rules is hard for a generalist to analyse.

b2.evidence: Total net revenue rose every year from $119.95B in 2020 to $182.4B in 2025, and it has stayed profitable through 2008, 2020 and 2023.

integrity.evidence: Dimon's shareholder letters are famously candid and capital allocation is disciplined, but the bank has paid large regulatory fines, such as about $920M for metals and Treasury spoofing in 2020.

b6.evidence: JPMorgan made opportunistic, low-priced acquisitions in crises (Bear Stearns, WaMu, First Republic) rather than empire-building at high prices.

roic.evidence: Return on tangible common equity was 20% and ROE 17% in 2025, best among large US banks, but this relies on the leverage inherent in banking.

fcf.evidence: Free cash flow is not a meaningful measure for a bank, but its earnings convert into capital returns: a net payout of 82% over the 12 months to end-2025 while keeping CET1 at 14.5%.

b10.evidence: Book value per share grew to $126.99 at end-2025 from $116.07 a year earlier, and the market value of about $880B is well above the earnings it retained.

safety.evidence: At $331.43 the shares trade at about 3.1 times tangible book value of $107.56 per share (Dec 2025), a premium rather than a discount to conservative value.

fairprice.evidence: About 14 times trailing and 13 times forward earnings is reasonable for a bank earning 20% on tangible equity, though high versus its own history on book value.

mu5.evidence: Fortress capital (13.9% CET1 in Sept 2026) and diversification limit the risk, but as a leveraged bank it could still be hurt by a severe credit crisis, trading loss or cyber attack.

reinvest.evidence: It can reinvest in new branches, technology and lending at high returns, but regulation and its size limit growth, so most profits are returned to shareholders.

ly2.evidence: JPMorgan is a stalwart with a simple story: the strongest, best-run large US bank gaining deposit and card share.

ly3.evidence: The P/E of about 14 is above its expected earnings growth rate, a PEG ratio of about 1.3 (StockAnalysis, Oct 2026).

runway.evidence: It is still adding branches in new states, wealth clients and Chase UK customers, but at $182.4B of revenue its growth will track the economy.

ly7.evidence: The share count fell about 3.7% over the past year through buybacks, but insiders, including Jamie Dimon in 2024, have been selling rather than buying.

ly8.evidence: JPMorgan is the largest US bank and one of the most widely followed stocks on Wall Street.

fi2.evidence: It keeps launching new offerings such as Chase UK, Kinexys blockchain payments and AI tools, though banking products themselves change slowly.

fi3.evidence: Banks do not report R&D, but JPMorgan's technology spending has produced a top-rated mobile app and leading payments platforms.

fi4.evidence: It ranks No. 1 in US retail deposits, credit card sales volume and global investment-banking fees, showing exceptional selling power.

longterm.evidence: Dimon keeps excess capital and invests heavily in technology and branches through cycles, accepting lower short-term returns for long-term strength.

gr1.evidence: It is the largest US bank, with $182.4B of 2025 revenue and a market value of about $880B.

ni10.evidence: JPMorgan earned a profit in every year of the last decade, from $24.4B in 2015 to $57.0B in 2025.

gr4.evidence: JPMorgan and its predecessors have paid a dividend every year for decades, including through 2009 when it cut the quarterly dividend to $0.05.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $6.00 in 2015 to $20.02 in 2025, more than tripling.

gr6.evidence: At $331.43 the price is about 16.6 times 2025 diluted EPS of $20.02 and about 16.7 times the 2024-2025 average, slightly above Graham's 15.

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 13.9 times P/B of about 2.6 gives about 36, above Graham's 22.5 limit.

th1.evidence: Its products (accounts, loans, trading) are similar to rivals'; its edge is scale and execution, not technology ten times better.

timing.evidence: Strong capital markets and possible looser capital rules favour it now, but falling rates could squeeze net interest income.

th3.evidence: Today's JPMorgan was formed by mergers of large banks (Chase, J.P. Morgan, Bank One) rather than by dominating a small niche.

team.evidence: Jamie Dimon and a deep bench of executives, including co-presidents Doug Petno and Troy Rohrbaugh, are widely seen as the best management team in banking.

th5.evidence: Branches reaching about 69% of the US population, a leading mobile app and relationships with most of the Fortune 500 give it unmatched distribution.

durable.evidence: Its deposit franchise, scale and regulatory barriers should keep it a leading bank in 10-20 years, though fintechs and private credit compete for parts of the business.

th7.evidence: JPMorgan's opportunities are well understood by competitors; it wins by execution rather than a unique insight.

trend.evidence: It is a heavy adopter of AI and digital payments, but it is not a leading beneficiary of a platform shift the way chip or cloud companies are.

dr1.evidence: Revenue reached $157.4B in the first nine months of 2026 and consensus FY2026 revenue rose to about $208B, but EPS grew only from $19.75 (2024) to $20.02 (2025).

dr2.evidence: Lighter capital rules and strong deal activity could lift returns, but a credit downturn or lower rates could offset them.

dr4.evidence: Higher rates have boosted net interest income, while falling rates and a weaker economy would reduce it even as investment banking recovers.

dr6.evidence: Changes to US capital rules, investment-banking fee recovery and the CEO succession are identifiable events that could move results and the stock.

dr7.evidence: It is the highest-quality big bank, but bank leverage and macro sensitivity argue against a very large concentrated position.

gm.evidence: Gross margin does not apply to a bank, but its pre-tax margin rose from 29.9% in 2020 to 39.8% in 2025.

fcfyield.evidence: Free cash flow is not meaningful for a bank; its earnings yield is about 7% (P/E about 13.9) and dividend yield about 2%.

gb2.evidence: Operating profit versus enterprise value is not meaningful for a bank, whose debt and cash are operating items.

pa2.evidence: JPMorgan is not in a setback; it earned a record $58.5B in 2024 and $57.0B in 2025.

pa4.evidence: Fortress capital makes permanent loss unlikely, but at about 3.1 times tangible book the shares could de-rate in a credit downturn.

wo1.evidence: It runs Kinexys, one of the largest bank blockchain platforms, and invests heavily in AI, but it is a bank rather than an innovation-platform leader.

wo2.evidence: Banking costs do not fall steeply with volume in a way that opens up large new demand.

wo3.evidence: It combines AI and blockchain in payments and operations, but these support its core banking rather than define it.

wo4.evidence: Its markets grow with the economy; consensus expects revenue growth in the single digits after 2026.

ac3.evidence: Its earnings depend heavily on interest rates, credit conditions and capital markets.

ns1.evidence: Its scale funds the best branch network and app and competitive rates, helping it take deposit share from 8.1% (2015) to 11.1% (2025), but it does not pursue a low-price strategy.

ns4.evidence: It is likely to keep gaining share, but CEO succession, fintechs and stablecoins make a clearly stronger position uncertain.

va2.evidence: It keeps money safe, moves trillions of dollars of payments a day and finances companies and households, a large and essential need.
